blocks.text: Raise the price of salt by twenty per cent and Nigerian households will still buy almost the same amount. Raise the price of one brand of noodles by twenty per cent and shoppers will reach for the brand beside it. The law of demand tells you which way quantity moves; elasticity tells you by how much.

blocks.markdown: **Elasticity of demand** measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in one of its determinants. The most important form is **price elasticity of demand (PED)**.

blocks.latex: PED = \frac{\text{percentage change in quantity demanded}}{\text{percentage change in price}}
blocks.caption: Price elasticity of demand. Because the two changes move in opposite directions the answer is negative, so we conventionally report its absolute value

blocks.title: Calculating PED and its effect on revenue
blocks.prompt: When the price of a bucket of garri rises from ₦500 to ₦600, quantity demanded falls from 200 buckets to 180 buckets per day. Calculate the price elasticity of demand, state its type, and work out what happens to total revenue.

steps.text: Percentage change in price: the rise is ₦600 − ₦500 = ₦100 on an original ₦500.
Percentage change in quantity demanded: the fall is 200 − 180 = 20 buckets on an original 200.
Divide and take the absolute value.
Since 0.5 lies between 0 and 1, demand for garri is inelastic — buyers cut back proportionately less than the price rose.
Total revenue before: ₦500 × 200 = ₦100,000. Total revenue after: ₦600 × 180 = ₦108,000. Revenue has risen by ₦8,000.
This confirms the rule: when demand is inelastic, a price rise increases total revenue.

blocks.answer: PED = 0.5, demand is inelastic, and total revenue rises from ₦100,000 to ₦108,000

blocks.title: Elasticity and total revenue
blocks.text: If demand is inelastic (PED < 1), raise the price to raise revenue. If demand is elastic (PED > 1), cut the price to raise revenue, because the extra sales more than make up for the lower price per unit. If PED = 1, revenue is at its maximum and a price change leaves it broadly unchanged.

blocks.markdown:
### What makes demand elastic or inelastic

- **Availability of close substitutes** — the more substitutes, the more elastic. This is why a single brand faces elastic demand while the commodity as a whole may not.
- **Proportion of income spent** — a matchbox takes a trivial share of income, so demand is inelastic; a motorcycle takes a large share, so demand is elastic.
- **Necessity or luxury** — necessities such as salt and staple food have inelastic demand; luxuries have elastic demand.
- **Time period** — demand is more elastic in the long run, because consumers have time to find alternatives.
- **Habit-forming goods** — cigarettes and similar goods have relatively inelastic demand.
- **Number of uses** — a commodity with many uses, such as electricity, has more elastic demand.
- **Postponability** — a purchase that can be delayed, such as repainting a house, has elastic demand.

### Income elasticity of demand (YED)

YED measures how demand responds to a change in consumer income:

$YED = \dfrac{\% \text{ change in quantity demanded}}{\% \text{ change in income}}$

If YED is **positive** the good is **normal**; if YED is greater than 1 it is a **luxury** or superior good; if YED is **negative** the good is **inferior**, meaning demand falls as people get richer.

**Worked figure**: a household's income rises from ₦50,000 to ₦60,000 a month, a rise of 20 per cent, and its purchase of beef rises from 4 kg to 5 kg, a rise of 25 per cent. YED = 25 ÷ 20 = **1.25**, so beef is a normal good and, being above 1, behaves as a luxury for this household.

### Cross elasticity of demand (XED)

XED measures how the demand for one good responds to a change in the price of another:

$XED = \dfrac{\% \text{ change in quantity demanded of good X}}{\% \text{ change in price of good Y}}$

A **positive** XED means the goods are **substitutes** — if the price of butter rises 10 per cent and the demand for margarine rises 20 per cent, XED = +2. A **negative** XED means they are **complements**. An XED of zero means the goods are unrelated.

### Price elasticity of supply (PES)

$PES = \dfrac{\% \text{ change in quantity supplied}}{\% \text{ change in price}}$

Because both changes go the same way, PES is normally positive. If the price of eggs rises from ₦300 to ₦360, a rise of 20 per cent, and quantity supplied rises from 50 to 65 crates, a rise of 30 per cent, then PES = 30 ÷ 20 = **1.5**, so supply is elastic.

Supply is more elastic when the good is easy to store, when production can be expanded quickly, when spare capacity exists, and when a long time period is allowed. Agricultural supply is highly inelastic in the short run because a growing season cannot be shortened.

blocks.title: Elasticity and taxation
blocks.text: When an indirect tax is placed on a good with inelastic demand, buyers cannot easily switch away, so most of the tax is passed on to them in a higher price. Where demand is elastic, the producer must absorb more of the tax or lose sales. This is exactly why governments target petroleum products, tobacco and alcohol for indirect taxes.

points: PED is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, reported as an absolute value.
PED below 1 is inelastic, above 1 is elastic, and exactly 1 is unitary.
With inelastic demand a price rise raises total revenue; with elastic demand a price cut raises total revenue.
Substitutes, share of income, necessity, time and postponability determine how elastic demand is.
Positive income elasticity indicates a normal good and negative income elasticity an inferior good.
Positive cross elasticity indicates substitutes and negative cross elasticity indicates complements.
Indirect taxes fall mainly on the consumer when demand is inelastic.
